subject: literature
passage: The novelist Edwin Marsh set most of his books in Hollins, a fictional mill town. Marsh himself grew up in Dunford, a real mill town in northern England. Literary scholar Aiko Tanaka claims that Hollins is closely modeled on Dunford and that Marsh changed little more than the name.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanaka's claim?

choices.A: Marsh wrote in a letter that he had invented Hollins so that no reader would recognize any real place.
choices.B: Maps of Dunford from Marsh's childhood match the streets, bridges, and mills of the Hollins novels almost exactly.
choices.C: Many novels of the period were set in fictional industrial towns with invented names.
choices.D: Marsh moved away from Dunford at eighteen and rarely returned to the town for the rest of his life.

explanation.why: Tanaka's claim is that the fictional Hollins copies the real Dunford in nearly every detail. The strongest support compares the two directly and finds them matching. A letter in which Marsh says he invented the town would weaken the claim rather than support it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A statement that Hollins was invented to avoid resembling any real place works against Tanaka's claim.
explanation.B: Correct. If the real town's layout matches the fictional one almost exactly, Hollins is indeed Dunford with a new name.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A general fashion for fictional towns says nothing about whether this particular town was based on Dunford.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Leaving Dunford does not show whether Marsh used it as the model for Hollins.
